course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
title: Exam 1 Review: Vectors, Matrices, Systems, Subspaces, Transformations, and Determinants
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
sessionGoal: Students should leave with a clean map of Exam 1 skills and practice the most common mixed problem types from the first part of the course.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Open with a topic map: vectors/matrices, systems/RREF, subspaces/bases, transformations, determinants.
Tell students the goal is not to memorize; it is to recognize the problem type quickly.
Do Problems 2, 3, and 5 if time is short.
For each problem, ask: what type of problem is this before solving?
End by pointing students to Practice Lab Sections 1-4 and Exam Mode.
sayThisFirst: Exam review is about recognition. First identify the problem type, then use the matching method.
For vector problems, ask: do I need a vector, a scalar, or a geometric interpretation?
For systems, row reduce and read pivots/free variables.
For subspaces and bases, ask: do I need span, independence, or both?
For transformations, remember columns are images of basis vectors.
boardPlan: Make a two-column board: Topic / What to do first.
List the five problem types in today’s review.
Work through the problems in order, but skip Problem 1 if students are already strong with vectors.
After each problem, write one takeaway sentence.
Leave the last 5 minutes for students to choose which Practice Lab sections to review.

examCoverageGuide.whatToRecognize: Component arithmetic, dot products, matrix dimensions, transposes.
Pivots, free variables, no solution vs infinitely many solutions.
Span membership equations and independence equations look similar but ask different things.
Build matrices from images of basis vectors and use Ax.
Use \(\det(A)\) to decide invertibility and track row operation effects.

commonMistakes: Not saying what type of problem it is before starting algebra.
Using RREF columns as a basis for \(\operatorname{Col}(A)\).
Mixing up span membership with linear independence.
Forgetting that T(e_i) values become columns.
For determinant parameter problems, giving the bad value instead of the invertible condition.
notationWarnings: Do not call \(\det(A)\) a matrix. It is a scalar.

problems.title: Vector warm-up: arithmetic and dot product meaning
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(u=(2,-1,2)\) and \(v=(1,3,0)\). Compute \(u+2v\), compute \(u\cdot v\), and decide whether the angle between \(u\) and \(v\) is acute, obtuse, or right.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: first check whether each answer should be a vector or a scalar.

drawInstructions: Draw two arrows from the origin labeled u and v.
Write dot product < 0 means the angle is obtuse.
Do not try to draw exact 3D coordinates; use the sign interpretation.

walkthrough.label: Interpret the angle
walkthrough.latex: Because \(u\cdot v<0\), the angle between them is obtuse.

problems.finalAnswerLatex: u+2v=(4,5,2),\qquad u\cdot v=-1,\qquad \text{the angle is obtuse.}
commonMistakes: Thinking dot product gives a vector.
Forgetting to multiply v by 2 before adding.
Only saying dot product is negative without interpreting the angle.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 1 for vector/matrix basics.

problems.title: Read a solution set from RREF
problems.studentPromptLatex:
The augmented matrix of a system row-reduces to
\[\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2&|&-1\\0&1&-3&|&4\\0&0&0&|&0\end{bmatrix}.\]
Write the solution set in parametric form.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: this problem is about reading, not more row reducing. Identify pivots and free variables first.

drawInstructions: Translate the first two rows into equations.
Box the final parametric vector form.

walkthrough.label: Identify pivot and free variables
walkthrough.latex: Pivots are in columns 1 and 2, so \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are pivot variables. Column 3 has no pivot, so let \(x_3=t\).

commonMistakes: Forgetting to introduce a parameter for \(x_3\).
Thinking the zero row means no solution. It does not.
Leaving the answer as equations without a clear solution set.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 2 for RREF and solution sets.

problems.title: Span, dependence, and a basis for the span
problems.studentPromptLatex:
Let
\[v_1=(1,0,2),\quad v_2=(0,1,-1),\quad v_3=(2,1,3),\quad b=(3,2,4).\]
Is \(b\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}\)? Are \(v_1,v_2,v_3\) linearly independent? Give a basis for their span.
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: this problem asks three related questions. Do not answer only the first one.

drawInstructions: Draw a plane through the origin spanned by \(v_1\) and \(v_2\).
Draw \(v_3\) inside the same plane and label \(v_3=2v_1+v_2\).
Draw b inside the same plane and label b=3v1+2v2.
Emphasize that \(v_3\) is redundant, so \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) form a basis for the span.

walkthrough.label: Check b is in the span
Decide independence
walkthrough.latex: Since \(v_3=2v_1+v_2\), one vector is made from the others. Therefore the set is linearly dependent.

walkthrough.label: Give a basis for the span
walkthrough.latex:
The vectors \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) are not multiples of each other, so they are independent. Since \(v_3\) is redundant, a basis is
\[\{v_1,v_2\}=\{(1,0,2),(0,1,-1)\}.\]

problems.finalAnswerLatex: b\in\operatorname{span}\{v_1,v_2,v_3\},\quad \{v_1,v_2,v_3\}\text{ is dependent},\quad \text{a basis for the span is }\{(1,0,2),(0,1,-1)\}.
commonMistakes: Answering span membership but forgetting independence.
Thinking dependent means b is not in the span. These are different questions.
Giving all three vectors as a basis even though \(v_3\) is redundant.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 3 for span, independence, and bases.

problems.title: Linear transformation and area scaling
skills: Use determinant for invertibility and area scaling
problems.studentPromptLatex:
Let \(T(x)=Ax\), where
\[A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&1\end{bmatrix}.\]
Compute \(T(2,-1)\). Is \(T\) one-to-one and onto? What is the area scale factor?
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: for a square 2 by 2 transformation, determinant answers invertibility and area scaling.

drawInstructions: Draw the unit square and its image as a parallelogram with area scale 5.
Write \(\det(A)=-5\), so orientation flips and area scales by 5.
Show T(2,-1) as a separate matrix-vector multiplication.

walkthrough.label: Interpret determinant
walkthrough.latex: Since \(\det(A)\neq 0\), \(T\) is one-to-one and onto. The area scale factor is \(|\det(A)|=5\). The negative sign means orientation is flipped.

problems.finalAnswerLatex: T(2,-1)=\begin{bmatrix}0\\5\end{bmatrix},\quad T\text{ is one-to-one and onto},\quad \text{area scale factor }=5.
commonMistakes: Forgetting absolute value for area scale.
Saying area scale is -5. Area cannot be negative.
Forgetting that determinant nonzero implies both one-to-one and onto for \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 4 for transformations and determinants.

problems.title: Parameter value for invertibility
problems.studentPromptLatex:
For what values of \(k\) is
\[M(k)=\begin{bmatrix}1&k&0\\2&1&1\\0&3&2\end{bmatrix}\]
invertible?
problems.whatToSayBefore: Tell students: this is a determinant problem. Invertible means det is not zero.

drawInstructions: After computing -4k-1, set it equal to zero to find the bad value.
Draw a number line with k=-1/4 marked as the only excluded value.

walkthrough.label: Find the bad value
walkthrough.latex:
The matrix is not invertible when
\[-1-4k=0.\]
So \(k=-\frac14\).

commonMistakes: Stopping at k=-1/4 without saying whether that is good or bad.
Forgetting the minus sign in cofactor expansion.
Saying determinant must equal 1. It only needs to be nonzero.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 4 and Exam Mode for more review.

wrapUpQuestions: Which topics still feel slow: RREF, span/bases, transformations, or determinants?
What is the first thing you do when you see an RREF matrix?
What does determinant nonzero tell you?
What Practice Lab section should you review next?

reviewSummary: Session 09 is the first exam review session. It has five mixed original problems covering Sections 1-4, with simple board-first explanations and exact visual specs.

open.title: Exam review is about recognition
say: Welcome to Exam 1 review. Most problems on this exam aren't hard once you know what kind they are. The tricky part is the first ten seconds: recognizing the type.
So today, for every problem, we'll say out loud: what type is this, and what's the first move? Then we do it.

ask.q: Quick poll: which topic feels slowest for you right now: row reduction, span and bases, transformations, or determinants?
ask.a: Note the answers on the board; spend extra time on the most common one.

write: vector/dot product → vector or number? sign of u · v
system → augmented matrix, row reduce, circle pivots
span / independence / basis → vectors as columns

idea.title: The five problem types on Exam 1
say: Almost every Exam 1 problem is one of these five types. Each has a first move that gets you going.
Vectors: decide whether the answer is a vector or a number, and use the sign of the dot product for angles. Systems: row reduce, then read pivots and free variables.

Span and independence: put the vectors in as columns and row reduce or take the determinant. Transformations: the columns of the matrix are where the basis vectors go. Determinants: nonzero means invertible, and |det| is the area or volume scale.
draw: Draw a two-column table titled 'Exam 1 map': Topic | First move.
Fill in the five rows from the Write list, one line each.
Leave room under each row for one takeaway sentence; fill it in after each problem.

ask.q: An exam problem gives you an RREF matrix. What's your first move?
ask.a: Circle the pivots and identify the free variables.

ask.q: A problem asks 'is T one-to-one?' for a 2 × 2 matrix. Fastest test?
ask.a: Compute the determinant; nonzero means one-to-one and onto.

launch.say: Warm-up: compute u + 2v and u · v, then decide if the angle is acute, obtuse or right. Label each answer vector or number.
circulate: Check that v was doubled before adding.
Push for the interpretation, not just 'the dot product is −1'.

askFirst.q: Which answers here are vectors and which are numbers?
askFirst.a: u + 2v is a vector; u · v is a number; the angle type is a word.

ask.q: What's the most common slip here?
ask.a: Adding v instead of 2v.

ask.q: Is −1 a small or large angle?
ask.a: Slightly over 90°, since the dot product is barely negative compared to the lengths.

steps.say: Negative dot product means cos θ < 0: the angle is obtuse.

ask.q: What would a dot product of 0 have meant?
ask.a: A right angle: perpendicular.

steps.why: The sign of the dot product answers the angle question without computing any angle.

si09-p1.meaning: u and v point just a bit more than perpendicular apart. On an exam, 'acute / obtuse / right' is always a sign check.

ifStuck.if: a student tries to compute the actual angle with arccos
ifStuck.then: point out the question only asks for the type; the sign is enough.

si09-p1.transition: Type two: systems. The row reduction is already done here, so it's pure reading.

launch.say: Write the solution set in parametric form. No more row reducing, just read.
circulate: Check the signs: x₁ + 2x₃ = −1 gives x₁ = −1 − 2t.
Anyone saying 'the zero row means no solution'? Ask them to read it as an equation.

askFirst.q: First move for an RREF problem?
askFirst.a: Circle the pivots, find the free variables.

steps.say: Pivots in columns 1 and 2. Column 3 is free: x₃ = t.

ask.q: How many solutions will there be?
ask.a: Infinitely many: one free variable, and no inconsistent row.

steps.say: Rows as equations: x₁ + 2x₃ = −1 and x₂ − 3x₃ = 4.

ask.q: What does the last row say?
ask.a: 0 = 0: no information, no problem.

steps.say: Move the t terms right: x₁ = −1 − 2t, x₂ = 4 + 3t.

ask.q: Why did −3x₃ become +3t?
ask.a: Moving it across the equals sign flips its sign.

steps.say: Write the whole solution as a triple in t. Or as a point plus t times a direction.

ask.q: What shape is this solution set?
ask.a: A line in ℝ³ through (−1, 4, 0) in direction (−2, 3, 1).

si09-p2.meaning: A line of solutions: one free variable means one direction of freedom.

ifStuck.then: ask what value x₃ has. It can be anything, so it needs a name.

si09-p2.transition: Type three: span, independence and bases, all asked at once.

launch.say: Three questions: is b in the span, are the vectors independent, and what's a basis for the span. Answer all three.
circulate: Look for students who spot v₃ = 2v₁ + v₂ by eye. Have them share.
Is anyone giving all three vectors as a basis?

askFirst.q: What's the difference between 'b is in the span' and 'the vectors are independent'?
askFirst.a: The first asks if some combination makes b; the second asks if any vector is redundant.

steps.say: Look for a relation first: 2v₁ + v₂ = (2, 1, 3) = v₃. So v₃ is redundant.

ask.q: How might you spot this without guessing?
ask.a: Row reduce [v₁ v₂ v₃]; column 3 won't be a pivot column.

steps.say: Now b: 3v₁ + 2v₂ = (3, 2, 4) = b. So b is in the span.

ask.q: Could b be in the span even though the vectors are dependent?
ask.a: Yes. These are separate questions.

steps.say: Because v₃ = 2v₁ + v₂, the set is dependent.

ask.q: Write a dependence relation equal to zero.
ask.a: 2v₁ + v₂ − v₃ = 0.

steps.say: v₁ and v₂ aren't multiples of each other, so {v₁, v₂} is independent and spans the same plane: that's a basis.

ask.q: What's the dimension of the span?
ask.a: 2: it's a plane through the origin.

steps.why: A basis for a span: keep the vectors that aren't redundant (the pivot columns).

si09-p3.meaning: All three vectors and b lie in one plane through the origin. Two directions describe it; the third vector was a duplicate direction.

ifStuck.if: a student thinks 'dependent' means 'b is not in the span'
ifStuck.then: separate the questions on the board, one per line.

si09-p3.transition: Type four: transformations and what the determinant tells us about them.

launch.say: Compute T(2, −1), decide one-to-one and onto, and find the area scale factor.
circulate: Watch for 'area scale is −5'. Area scale is the absolute value.

askFirst.q: For a square matrix, which single number answers 'one-to-one and onto'?

ask.q: Say it as columns.
ask.a: 2 times column 1 minus column 2.

ask.q: What does the minus sign mean?
ask.a: The transformation flips orientation.

steps.say: Nonzero determinant: one-to-one and onto. Area scale factor is |−5| = 5.

ask.q: A triangle of area 2 goes through T. New area?

steps.why: The determinant's size scales area; its sign says whether the picture is mirrored.

si09-p4.meaning: T stretches every region's area by 5 and mirrors it. Nothing collapses, so T can be undone.

ifStuck.then: ask whether an area can be negative.

si09-p4.transition: Last type: a parameter, and the one value of k that breaks invertibility.

launch.say: For which k is M(k) invertible? Classic exam problem.
circulate: Check the minus sign on the middle cofactor.
Make sure final answers say k ≠ −1/4, not k = −1/4.

askFirst.q: What equation finds the bad k?

steps.say: Expand along row 1. The 0 in the top-right corner kills the third term.

ask.q: Why expand along row 1?
ask.a: It has a zero, and the k is in it.

steps.say: The minors are 2 − 3 = −1 and 4 − 0 = 4. So det M = −1 − 4k.

ask.q: Check: at k = 0, is M invertible?
ask.a: det = −1 ≠ 0, so yes.

steps.say: −1 − 4k = 0 gives k = −1/4, the one bad value.

ask.q: What happens to M's columns at k = −1/4?
ask.a: They become dependent.

ask.q: How many good values of k are there?
ask.a: Infinitely many: all reals except one.

si09-p5.meaning: Exactly one value of k flattens the box the columns span; everywhere else M is invertible.

ifStuck.then: remind them invertible means det ≠ 0, not det = 1.

wrap.write: Recognize the type → make the first move → check the answer means what the question asked.

exit.q: What's the first thing you do with an RREF matrix?
What does det ≠ 0 tell you about a square matrix?
exit.a: It's invertible: the columns are independent and T is one-to-one and onto.

exit.q: Which Practice Lab section will you review next, and why?
exit.a: Use the poll from the start: point each student to Sections 1–4 by their weakest topic.

wrap.next: Good luck on Exam 1. After it: matrix inverses, and then eigenvalues, the core of the second unit.
